## Introduction

Many responses in applied work are counts: the number of doctor visits in a
year, articles published, defects on a production line. The standard model
for counts is Poisson regression, which assumes that the variance of each
count equals its mean. Real counts are usually more spread out than that,
which is called **overdispersion**, and they often contain **more zeros**
than a Poisson model allows [@cameron2013]. Ignoring either problem gives
standard errors that are too small and predictions that miss the zeros.

Two models address these problems. **Negative binomial (NB) regression**
adds a dispersion parameter $\theta$, so the variance becomes
$\mu + \mu^2/\theta$. The **zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB)** model
goes further: it treats the data as a mixture of a group that always
produces zeros and a group whose counts follow an NB regression
[@lambert1992]. In R, these models are usually fitted with
`MASS::glm.nb()` [@venables2002] and `pscl::zeroinfl()` [@zeileis2008].

This project builds an R package, **nbzinbreg**, that fits both models
without any general-purpose optimizer. The NB model is fitted by
iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) for the regression coefficients,
alternated with Newton–Raphson for $\theta$. The ZINB model is fitted by an
EM algorithm whose M-steps are IRLS fits. The report describes the methods
(@sec-methods) and the package (@sec-package). It then shows that the
package reproduces `glm.nb()` and `zeroinfl()` (@sec-benchmark) and that
`zinbreg()` recovers known parameters in a simulation (@sec-simulation). It
analyses physician visits in the NMES1988 data (@sec-nmes) and ends with a
discussion of limitations (@sec-discussion).

## Methods {#sec-methods}

**The NB model.** For counts $y_i$ with covariates $x_i$, an optional
offset $o_i$ and prior weights $a_i$ (1 for an ordinary fit), the NB2 model
has mean $\mu_i = \exp(\eta_i)$ with linear predictor
$\eta_i = x_i^\top\beta + o_i$, and log-likelihood

$$
\ell(\beta, \theta) = \sum_i a_i \Big[\log\Gamma(y_i + \theta) -
\log\Gamma(\theta) - \log y_i! + \theta\log\theta + y_i\log\mu_i -
(\theta + y_i)\log(\theta + \mu_i)\Big].
$$ {#eq-nb-ll}

This is the parameterization of `glm.nb()`. As $\theta \to \infty$ the
model becomes the Poisson.

**IRLS for $\beta$ with $\theta$ fixed.** With $\theta$ held fixed, the NB
model is a generalized linear model with log link and variance function
$V(\mu) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta$. Fisher scoring for such a model is the same
as repeating a weighted least-squares fit, with weights and a "working
response"

$$
w_i = a_i\,\frac{\theta\mu_i}{\theta + \mu_i}, \qquad
z_i = (\eta_i - o_i) + \frac{y_i - \mu_i}{\mu_i}, \qquad
\beta^{\text{new}} = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W z.
$$ {#eq-irls}

The solution is computed from the QR decomposition of $\sqrt{W}X$, not by
inverting $X^\top WX$. A step that would lower the log-likelihood is halved
back towards the current $\beta$.

**Newton–Raphson for $\theta$ with $\beta$ fixed.** Write $U(\theta)$ and
$H(\theta)$ for the first and second derivatives of @eq-nb-ll in $\theta$;
they involve the digamma and trigamma functions. The update works on
$\phi = \log\theta$, which keeps $\theta$ positive:

$$
U_\phi = \theta\,U(\theta), \qquad
H_\phi = \theta^2 H(\theta) + \theta\,U(\theta), \qquad
\phi^{\text{new}} = \phi - U_\phi / H_\phi .
$$ {#eq-nr}

If $H_\phi$ is not negative (the log-likelihood is not hill-shaped there),
a scaled uphill step is used instead, and every step must pass a line search
that guarantees an increase in the log-likelihood.

**The NB outer loop and standard errors.** The fit starts from a Poisson
IRLS fit and a moment estimate of $\theta$, then alternates @eq-irls and
@eq-nr until the relative change in the log-likelihood is below $10^{-8}$
and the coefficients and $\log\theta$ have stopped moving. As in `glm.nb()`,
$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (X^\top \hat W X)^{-1}$, treating
$\theta$ as known, and
$\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta) = \{-H(\hat\theta)\}^{-1/2}$.

**The ZINB model.** Each person is a *structural zero* with probability
$\pi_i$, with $\operatorname{logit}\pi_i = z_i^\top\gamma$; otherwise the
count follows the NB model above. With
$f_0 = \{\theta/(\theta + \mu_i)\}^\theta$ the NB probability of a zero, the
observed-data log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\beta, \gamma, \theta) = \sum_{y_i = 0} a_i \log\big[\pi_i + (1 -
\pi_i) f_0\big] + \sum_{y_i > 0} a_i \Big[\log(1 - \pi_i) + \log
f_{\text{NB}}(y_i; \mu_i, \theta)\Big].
$$ {#eq-zinb-ll}

The first sum mixes the two sources of zeros inside a logarithm, so the
ZINB model is not a GLM and cannot be fitted by IRLS directly.

**EM.** If we knew which zeros were structural, the model would split into
two ordinary regressions. The EM algorithm [@dempster1977] treats that
label as missing and alternates two steps. The **E-step** computes, for each
zero, the probability that it is structural, given the current estimates:

$$
\tau_i = \frac{\pi_i}{\pi_i + (1 - \pi_i) f_0} \quad (y_i = 0), \qquad
\tau_i = 0 \quad (y_i > 0).
$$ {#eq-estep}

The **M-step** then fits the two regressions with these probabilities as
weights. The zero part is a logistic regression of the fractional response
$\tau_i$ on $z_i$, fitted by IRLS; each round solves
$(Z^\top VZ)\,\Delta = Z^\top A(\tau - \pi)$ with
$V = \operatorname{diag}\{a_i\pi_i(1 - \pi_i)\}$, the same Fisher-scoring
step written so that nothing is divided by $\pi_i(1 - \pi_i)$, which can
underflow. The count part is exactly the NB fit above, with prior weights
$a_i(1 - \tau_i)$, so the NB code is reused. All of these quantities are
computed on the log scale.

**Monotonicity and convergence.** EM can never lower the observed-data
log-likelihood. The package checks this at every iteration, together with
each M-step's own objective, and a decrease (beyond rounding) is reported
and blocks convergence; the check cannot be switched off. EM converges
slowly near the maximum, so small changes alone are a poor stopping rule:
the fit stops only when the relative change in the log-likelihood is below
$10^{-8}$, the parameters are stable, and the **Newton decrement**
$\delta = g^\top(-H)^{-1}g$ (with $g$ and $H$ the gradient and Hessian of
@eq-zinb-ll) is at most $10^{-8}$. This establishes approximate
stationarity. $\delta$ can only be computed where $-H$ is positive
definite, so a converged fit also has negative definite curvature: a local
maximum, not necessarily the highest one.

**Standard errors for ZINB.** EM gives no standard errors. They come from
the inverse of the observed information, $-H$, the negative Hessian of
@eq-zinb-ll in $(\beta, \gamma, \log\theta)$ at the estimates. The package
computes $H$ **analytically**, from closed-form derivatives of each
observation's contribution, and offers `numDeriv::hessian()` of our own
log-likelihood as an option; the two agree to about $10^{-11}$. Before
inverting, the Hessian is checked to be finite, symmetric and negative
definite. As in `zeroinfl()`, $\log\theta$ is reported with its standard
error, and $\theta$ with the delta-method standard error
$\theta \cdot \operatorname{SE}(\log\theta)$.

## The R package {#sec-package}

The package is installed from GitHub:

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("jaxsonbugg/nbzinbreg")
```

`nbreg()` and `zinbreg()` take `formula, data, offset, control` in that
order, as the project requires. A `zinbreg()` formula has the form
`y ~ x1 + x2 | z1 + z2`, with the count covariates before the bar and the
zero covariates after it. `nbreg_control()` and `zinbreg_control()` set
the tolerances, iteration limits, tracing and the Hessian method. Both
classes have `print`, `summary`, `coef`, `vcov`, `logLik` (so `AIC()` and
`BIC()` work), `fitted`, `residuals` (response and Pearson), `nobs` and
`predict` with `newdata` (for ZINB the types `response`, `count`, `zero`
and `prob`, with standard errors). Beyond the requirements, the package
offers `confint()` with a profile interval for $\theta$, `anova()`,
`overdispersion_test()`, `vuong_test()` with a parametric bootstrap test of
NB against ZINB, `expected_counts()`, `rootogram()`, `simulate()`,
`boot_se()`, `tidy()` and `glance()`.

A short example, with the bioChemists data used in the project handout:

```{r}
#| label: usage
#| echo: true
library(nbzinbreg)
data("bioChemists", package = "pscl")
fit <- zinbreg(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment | ment,
               data = bioChemists)
round(c(coef(fit), theta = fit$theta), 3)
```

**Design and testing.** The user-facing functions check every input and
give classed errors that say how to fix the problem; the numerical engines
never warn but return flags (for example $\theta$ at its Poisson-limit
bound), and the ZINB count M-step reuses the NB engine. The tests, run on
five platforms in GitHub Actions, compare both models with `glm.nb()` and
`zeroinfl()`, check offsets, single-covariate models, bad input and the
analytic Hessian, and read the package's own code to fail if any function
calls a prohibited optimizer or fitter, directly or indirectly.

## Benchmarking {#sec-benchmark}

```{r}
#| label: bench-setup
#| include: false
# The benchmark functions are installed with the package
# (inst/benchmark/benchmark_functions.R); the same code produced the saved
# timings. The agreement tables below are computed now, at render time,
# from the installed package; the timings are read from the saved results
# of inst/benchmark/benchmark.R, because repeated timing runs would make
# rendering slow and the numbers would change with every render.
library(nbzinbreg)
bench_file <- system.file("benchmark", "benchmark_functions.R",
                          package = "nbzinbreg")
source(bench_file)
specs <- bench_specs()
pairs <- lapply(specs, fit_pair, hessian = "analytic")
bench <- compare_pairs(pairs)
names(bench$tables) <- vapply(specs, `[[`, "", "id")
req <- bench$required

saved_file <- system.file("benchmark", "benchmark_results.rds",
                          package = "nbzinbreg")
saved <- if (nzchar(saved_file)) readRDS(saved_file)
prov_check <- if (!is.null(saved)) check_saved_provenance(saved$provenance)

fmt_est <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, digits = 7, format = "g"))
fmt_diff <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, digits = 1, format = "e"))
side_table <- function(id) {
  tab <- bench$tables[[id]]
  out <- data.frame(
    Parameter = tab$parameter,
    Ours = fmt_est(tab$estimate_ours),
    Reference = fmt_est(tab$estimate_reference),
    `|Diff.|` = fmt_diff(tab$estimate_abs_diff),
    `SE ours` = fmt_est(tab$se_ours),
    `SE ref.` = fmt_est(tab$se_reference),
    `SE |diff.|` = fmt_diff(tab$se_abs_diff),
    check.names = FALSE)
  kbl(out, align = "lrrrrrr")
}
max_of <- function(model, quantity) {
  max(req$max_abs_diff[req$model == model & req$quantity == quantity])
}
n_checks <- vapply(bench$validity, nrow, 1L)
all_valid <- all(vapply(bench$validity, pair_valid, logical(1)))
all_passed <- all(req$passed)
ll_higher <- req$note[req$quantity == "log-likelihood"]
```

The package should reproduce `MASS::glm.nb()` and
`pscl::zeroinfl(dist = "negbin")`. Each model is fitted to two data sets
with both implementations: `pscl::bioChemists` (915 PhD students; response
`art`; `fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment` in the count part and, for ZINB, in
the zero part, as in Appendix A of the project description) and
`AER::NMES1988` (the models of @sec-nmes). Our functions run at their
**default** settings; the references run with **tight** tolerances
(`glm.control(epsilon = 1e-10, maxit = 100)`,
`zeroinfl.control(reltol = 1e-12)`), so that their own stopping error is
negligible. Agreement then shows that both implementations reach the same
tightly converged estimates; it does not show that these are the global
maximum of the likelihood. For every coefficient, standard error, theta (log theta for
ZINB, as `zeroinfl()` estimates it) and the log-likelihood, the *maximum
absolute difference* |ours − reference| is compared with the required
tolerance: 1e-5 for NB coefficients and standard errors, 1e-4 for NB theta
and log-likelihood, and 1e-3 for every ZINB quantity.

A comparison is only meaningful if both fits are valid, so each pair is
checked first: both converged (for `zinbreg()` including the gradient
check), every estimate and standard error is finite, both use the same
observations and parameter names, and both covariance matrices are
symmetric and positive definite.
`r if (all_valid) sprintf("All %d checks passed for each of the four pairs.", n_checks[[1]]) else "**Not all checks passed; see the validity tables in the supplementary benchmark article.**"`
The side-by-side tables of every estimate and standard error are in the
appendix (@tbl-bench-bc-nb, @tbl-bench-nmes-nb, @tbl-bench-bc-zinb and
@tbl-bench-nmes-zinb).

@tbl-bench-summary collects the maximum absolute differences and compares
them with the required tolerances.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bench-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Maximum absolute differences from the reference fits, against the required tolerances."
#| echo: false
#| tbl-colwidths: false
summ <- data.frame(
  Data = sub("_.*", "", req$pair), Model = req$model, Quantity = req$quantity,
  `Max. abs. difference` = fmt_diff(req$max_abs_diff),
  Tolerance = formatC(req$tolerance, format = "e", digits = 0),
  Met = ifelse(req$passed, "yes", "NO"), check.names = FALSE)
kbl(summ, align = "lllrrc")
```

`r if (all_passed) "Every required quantity is within its tolerance" else "**Not every required quantity is within its tolerance**"`,
with a large margin: the largest differences are
`r fmt_diff(max_of("NB", "coefficients"))` for the NB coefficients and
`r fmt_diff(max_of("ZINB", "coefficients"))` for the ZINB coefficients.
The NB fits agree almost to rounding error (closely related algorithms
for the same likelihood). The ZINB differences are larger but still at
least `r floor(1e-3 / max(req$max_abs_diff[req$model == "ZINB"]))`
times below the tolerance: `zinbreg()` stops when its gradient check
places every estimate within a tiny fraction of a standard error of a
stationary point, `zeroinfl()` by its own BFGS criterion. The log-likelihoods differ by at most
`r fmt_diff(max_of("ZINB", "log-likelihood"))`;
`r if (all(grepl("reference is higher", ll_higher))) "in all four comparisons the reference value is very slightly higher" else "the higher value is reported per pair in the table"`.


```{r}
#| label: bench-time-numbers
#| include: false
med <- function(spec, pattern) {
  if (is.null(saved)) return(NA_real_)
  t <- saved$timing
  t$median_s[t$spec == spec & grepl(pattern, t$fit, fixed = TRUE)][1]
}
ratio_bc <- med("bioChemists_ZINB", "zinbreg() (default settings, analytic") /
  med("bioChemists_ZINB", "zeroinfl() (default")
ratio_nm <- med("NMES1988_ZINB", "zinbreg() (default settings, analytic") /
  med("NMES1988_ZINB", "zeroinfl() (default")
p <- if (!is.null(saved)) saved$provenance
zinb_pairs <- Filter(function(x) x$model == "ZINB", pairs)
em_iter <- vapply(zinb_pairs, function(x) x$ours$fit$iter, 1L)
bfgs <- vapply(zinb_pairs, function(x) {
  as.integer(x$ref$fit$optim$counts[["gradient"]])
}, 1L)
names(em_iter) <- names(bfgs) <- vapply(zinb_pairs, `[[`, "", "spec_id")
```

**Computation time** (median of 10 runs with `bench::mark()`;
@tbl-bench-time in the appendix). The NB fits take a fraction of a second
with either implementation. Our ZINB fits are about `r round(ratio_bc)`
(bioChemists) and `r round(ratio_nm)` (NMES1988) times slower than
`zeroinfl()` at its defaults: EM gains a roughly fixed fraction per
iteration, so it needed `r em_iter[["bioChemists_ZINB"]]` and
`r em_iter[["NMES1988_ZINB"]]` iterations of full IRLS fits, against
`r bfgs[["bioChemists_ZINB"]]` and `r bfgs[["NMES1988_ZINB"]]` gradient
evaluations for the BFGS search of `zeroinfl()`. Further, ungraded checks
are in the supplementary benchmark article on the package website.

## Simulation study {#sec-simulation}

```{r}
#| label: sim-setup
#| include: false
# The simulation (inst/benchmark/simulation.R) takes about 20 minutes, so
# its saved results are read here; the functions that produced them are
# installed with the package (inst/benchmark/simulation_functions.R).
source(system.file("benchmark", "simulation_functions.R", package = "nbzinbreg"))
sim_file <- system.file("benchmark", "simulation_results.rds",
                        package = "nbzinbreg")
sim <- if (nzchar(sim_file)) readRDS(sim_file)
sim_ok <- !is.null(sim)
if (sim_ok) {
  ss <- sim$summary
  st <- sim$settings
  cls <- sim$classes$counts
  prof <- sim$profile
  mom <- sim$design_moments
  sim_prov <- sim$provenance
  sim_check <- check_saved_provenance(sim_prov)
  sim_check$message <- gsub("the timings", "the simulation results",
                            sim_check$message, fixed = TRUE)
  row <- function(p) ss[ss$parameter == p, ]
  pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
  # estimate with its Monte Carlo SE, the SE to one significant digit
  pm <- function(x, se, d = 3) {
    sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f (%s)"), x, formatC(se, digits = 1, format = "fg"))
  }
  n_nonusable <- st$R - cls[["usable"]]
  # parameters whose coverage is more than 2 MC SEs from 95%
  off <- ss$parameter[abs(ss$coverage - 0.95) > 2 * ss$coverage_mcse]
  ratio_range <- range(ss$se_ratio)
  zmax <- max(abs(ss$bias / ss$bias_mcse))
}
```

The simulation fits `zinbreg()` to data generated from a ZINB model with
known parameters and compares the estimates with the truth.

**Design.** Each data set has n = `r if (sim_ok) st$n` observations with
three covariates: x1 ~ N(0, 1), used in both parts; x2 ~ Bernoulli(0.5),
used in the count part only; and z ~ N(0, 1), used in the zero part only.
The covariates are drawn once and kept fixed (a *fixed design*); only the
responses are redrawn, so the results describe the estimator for this
design. The true model is

$$\log \mu_i = 1 + 0.5\,x_{1i} - 0.5\,x_{2i}, \qquad
\operatorname{logit} \pi_i = -0.8 + 0.6\,x_{1i} - 0.5\,z_i, \qquad
\theta = 1.5.$$

Each observation is a structural zero with probability $\pi_i$ and otherwise
a negative binomial count with mean $\mu_i$ and dispersion $\theta$. Over
this design `r if (sim_ok) pct(mom[["zero_share"]])` of the observations
are expected to be zero, and `r if (sim_ok) pct(mom[["structural_share_of_zeros"]])`
of those zeros are structural (in the simulated data:
`r if (sim_ok) pct(sim$observed[["zero_share"]])` zeros). We simulated
R = `r if (sim_ok) format(st$R, big.mark = ",")` data sets (seed
`r if (sim_ok) st$seed`; data set r uses seed `r if (sim_ok) st$seed` + r, so
any one of them can be reproduced alone) and fitted each with
`zinbreg(y ~ x1 + x2 | x1 + z)`, the correct model, at its default settings.

**What is reported.** For each parameter: the **bias** (average estimate
minus the true value); the **Monte Carlo SD**, the actual spread of the
estimates; the **mean estimated SE** and its ratio to the Monte Carlo SD
(close to 1 if the standard errors are right); and the **coverage** of the
95% Wald intervals (estimate ± 1.96 SE). Every number has a **Monte Carlo
standard error** (MC SE, in parentheses), the uncertainty left because only
R data sets were simulated: exact for averages and coverage, and from
`r if (sim_ok) format(st$B, big.mark = ",")` bootstrap resamples of the
replications for the SD and the SE ratio. Theta is reported both as
log(theta), which `zinbreg()` estimates, and as theta, with the interval
theta ± 1.96 SE(theta). @tbl-sim gives the bias, spread,
standard errors and coverage; the relative bias and RMSE (@tbl-sim-rmse) and
the standardized errors (@fig-sim-z) are in the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sim
#| tbl-cap: "Simulation results over the usable replications: bias, the spread of the estimates against the reported standard errors, and the coverage of 95% Wald intervals (in %). Monte Carlo standard errors in parentheses."
#| echo: false
#| tbl-colwidths: false
if (sim_ok) {
  kbl(data.frame(
    Parameter = ss$parameter,
    Truth = formatC(ss$truth, digits = 3, format = "f"),
    Bias = pm(ss$bias, ss$bias_mcse),
    `MC SD` = pm(ss$mc_sd, ss$mc_sd_mcse),
    `Mean SE` = pm(ss$mean_se, ss$mean_se_mcse),
    `SE / SD` = pm(ss$se_ratio, ss$se_ratio_mcse, 2),
    `Coverage (%)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", 100 * ss$coverage,
                             100 * ss$coverage_mcse),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrrrr")
} else {
  cat("The saved simulation results were not found in the installed package; run inst/benchmark/simulation.R.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-results-text
#| include: false
# Every statement below is chosen from the numbers, so the text cannot
# claim more than the results show.
results_text <- if (sim_ok) {
  usable_txt <- sprintf(paste(
    "Of the %s fits, %s %s usable: converged with a passed gradient check,",
    "no estimate on a boundary, a valid covariance matrix, and finite,",
    "ordered intervals%s."),
    format(st$R, big.mark = ","), format(cls[["usable"]], big.mark = ","),
    if (cls[["usable"]] == 1) "was" else "were",
    if (n_nonusable > 0) sprintf(paste(
      "; the other %d are listed with their reasons in the saved results.",
      "Counting them as not covering, or as covering, puts the coverages",
      "between %s and %s"), n_nonusable,
      pct(min(ss$coverage_lower_bound)), pct(max(ss$coverage_upper_bound)))
    else " (none failed or ended on a boundary)")
  bias_se <- max(abs(ss$bias) / ss$mean_se)
  bias_txt <- if (zmax <= 3) sprintf(paste(
    "No bias is distinguishable from simulation noise (the largest is %.1f",
    "Monte Carlo SEs from zero), and every bias is below %s of a standard",
    "error."), zmax, pct(bias_se, 0)) else sprintf(paste(
    "Some biases are larger than simulation noise (up to %.1f Monte Carlo",
    "SEs from zero, for %s), although every bias is below %s of a standard",
    "error. This is the small-sample bias that maximum likelihood estimates",
    "have, of order 1/n: it is largest for the zero part and theta, which",
    "the data determine least precisely, and it shrinks as n grows (a",
    "check at n = 2000 is in the project notes)."), zmax,
    ss$parameter[which.max(abs(ss$bias / ss$bias_mcse))], pct(bias_se, 0))
  ratio_txt <- if (ratio_range[1] >= 0.9 && ratio_range[2] <= 1.1) sprintf(
    paste("The reported standard errors match the actual spread of the",
          "estimates: the SE/SD ratios lie between %.2f and %.2f."),
    ratio_range[1], ratio_range[2]) else sprintf(paste(
    "The SE/SD ratios lie between %.2f and %.2f, so for some parameters",
    "the reported standard errors and the actual spread differ by more than",
    "10%%."), ratio_range[1], ratio_range[2])
  cov_txt <- if (length(off)) sprintf(paste(
    "The coverage is within two Monte Carlo SEs of 95%% for every parameter",
    "except %s (%s)."), paste(off, collapse = ", "),
    paste(pct(ss$coverage[ss$parameter %in% off]), collapse = ", ")) else
    "The coverage of every 95% Wald interval is within two Monte Carlo SEs of 95%."
  et <- sim$replicates$estimate_theta[sim$replicates$class == "usable"]
  skew <- function(x) mean(((x - mean(x)) / stats::sd(x))^3)
  cl <- row("log(theta)")$coverage
  ct <- row("theta")$coverage
  theta_txt <- sprintf(paste(
    "For theta, the interval built on the log scale and transformed back",
    "covers %s of the time, and theta ± 1.96 SE(theta) %s. The estimates of",
    "theta are skewed (skewness %.2f; %.2f for log theta)%s."),
    pct(cl), pct(ct), skew(et), skew(log(et)),
    if (abs(cl - 0.95) < abs(ct - 0.95)) {
      ", and the log scale, where they are closer to normal, gives the more accurate interval"
    } else if (abs(cl - 0.95) > abs(ct - 0.95)) {
      ", although here the theta-scale interval is closer to 95%"
    } else "")
  paste(usable_txt, bias_txt, ratio_txt, cov_txt, theta_txt)
} else ""
```

**Results.** `r results_text`

```{r}
#| label: sim-profile-text
#| include: false
prof_text <- if (sim_ok) {
  sprintf(paste(
    "The profile-likelihood interval for theta from `confint()` was computed",
    "for the first %d data sets: %d were finite, %d unbounded above",
    "(certified), and %d could not be evaluated. Its coverage over the %d",
    "evaluable intervals is %s (MC SE %s)%s."),
    prof$n, prof$counts[["finite"]], prof$counts[["unbounded"]],
    prof$n - prof$evaluable, prof$evaluable, pct(prof$coverage),
    pct(prof$coverage_mcse),
    if (prof$n > prof$evaluable) sprintf(
      "; counting the others as not covering or covering gives %s to %s",
      pct(prof$lower_bound), pct(prof$upper_bound)) else "")
} else ""
# Profile intervals that failed because the profile search found a higher
# likelihood than the fit: the fit had stopped at a local maximum.
local_max <- if (sim_ok) {
  d <- sim$replicates$profile_detail
  which(!is.na(d) & grepl("not at its maximum", d, fixed = TRUE))
} else integer()
local_text <- if (length(local_max)) sprintf(paste(
  "In %s (data set %s), `confint()` refused to give an interval because its",
  "search over theta found a higher likelihood than the fit: `zinbreg()`",
  "had converged, with its gradient check passed, to a local maximum. Excess",
  "zeros can be explained either by zero inflation or by overdispersion, and",
  "the ZINB likelihood can have a maximum for each; EM finds the one its",
  "starting values lead to. The other fits passed the same checks, which",
  "establish a local maximum but not the highest one, so a small share of",
  "them may also be lower local maxima."),
  if (length(local_max) == 1L) "one case" else paste(length(local_max), "cases"),
  paste(sim$replicates$replication[local_max], collapse = ", ")) else ""
```

The fits took a median of
`r if (sim_ok) sprintf("%.2f", stats::median(sim$replicates$seconds))` s and
`r if (sim_ok) stats::median(sim$replicates$iterations)` EM iterations each. Profile-likelihood intervals for theta are summarized in the
appendix.

## Data analysis: NMES1988 {#sec-nmes}

```{r}
#| label: nmes-setup
#| include: false
# The fits are computed now, at render time, from the installed package
# (about 10 s); the slow bootstrap test (inst/benchmark/nmes_bootstrap.R,
# about 7 hours) is read from its saved results.
source(system.file("benchmark", "nmes_functions.R", package = "nbzinbreg"))
boot_file <- system.file("benchmark", "nmes_bootstrap_results.rds",
                         package = "nbzinbreg")
boot <- if (nzchar(boot_file)) readRDS(boot_file)
boot_ok <- !is.null(boot)
nm_maxit <- if (boot_ok) boot$settings$maxit else 5000L
nm_data <- nmes_data()
nm_desc <- nmes_descriptives(nm_data)
nm_fits <- nmes_fits(nm_data, maxit = nm_maxit)
nm_cmp <- nmes_comparison(nm_fits)
nm_irr_nb <- nmes_effects(nm_fits$nb, "count")
nm_irr_zi <- nmes_effects(nm_fits$zinb, "count")
nm_or <- nmes_effects(nm_fits$zinb, "zero")
nm_th_nb <- nmes_theta(nm_fits$nb)
nm_th_zi <- nmes_theta(nm_fits$zinb)
nm_od <- overdispersion_test(nm_fits$nb)
nm_vu <- vuong_test(nm_fits$zinb, nm_fits$nb)
nm_tabs <- lapply(nm_fits[c("poisson", "nb", "zinb")], nmes_count_table,
                  max_count = 30L)
if (boot_ok) {
  boot_check <- check_saved_provenance(boot$provenance)
  boot_check$message <- gsub("the timings", "the bootstrap results",
                             boot_check$message, fixed = TRUE)
  # the fits in the report must be the fits the bootstrap used
  stopifnot(identical(nmes_fit_hash(nm_fits$nb, nm_fits$zinb),
                      boot$header$fit_hash))
}
cm <- function(m, col) nm_cmp[nm_cmp$model == m, col]
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
ci2 <- function(lo, hi) sprintf("%s to %s", f2(lo), f2(hi))
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
# observed minus expected frequency at a count k, for one model
gap <- function(m, k) nm_tabs[[m]]$observed[k + 1] - nm_tabs[[m]]$expected[k + 1]
abs_err <- function(m) sum(abs(gap(m, 1:30)))
```

```{r}
#| label: nmes-claims
#| include: false
# Claim guards: every qualitative statement in the text below is checked
# here. If new results contradict one, rendering stops instead of leaving a
# false sentence in the report.
stopifnot(
  nm_desc$variance_to_mean > 5,                    # strongly overdispersed
  cm("poisson", "expected_zeros") < 0.1 * nm_desc$observed_zeros,
  cm("poisson", "expected_zeros") > nm_desc$poisson_unconditional_zeros,
  cm("nb", "expected_zeros") < nm_desc$observed_zeros,      # NB too few zeros
  cm("zinb", "expected_zeros") > nm_desc$observed_zeros,    # ZINB slightly too many
  abs(cm("zinb", "expected_zeros") - nm_desc$observed_zeros) <
    abs(cm("nb", "expected_zeros") - nm_desc$observed_zeros),
  gap("nb", 1) < 0, gap("nb", 2) < 0,              # NB: too many 1s and 2s
  abs_err("zinb") < abs_err("nb"),                 # ZINB closer above zero too
  cm("zinb", "AIC") < cm("nb", "AIC"),             # both criteria favour ZINB
  cm("zinb", "BIC") < cm("nb", "BIC"),
  cm("zinb_health", "AIC") > cm("zinb", "AIC"),    # health adds nothing
  cm("zinb_health", "BIC") > cm("zinb", "BIC"),
  nm_od$p.value < 1e-10,
  all(nm_vu$statistic > 2),
  all(nm_or$p_value[nm_or$term != "hospital"] < 0.01),
  nm_or$p_value[nm_or$term == "hospital"] > 0.05,
  all(nm_irr_zi$p_value < 0.01),
  # the NB effects are further from 1 than the ZINB count effects
  all(abs(log(nm_irr_nb$ratio)) >=
        abs(log(nm_irr_zi$ratio[match(nm_irr_nb$term, nm_irr_zi$term)]))),
  # chronic illness and insurance: less likely a non-user, more visits
  nm_or$ratio[nm_or$term == "chronic"] < 1,
  nm_or$ratio[nm_or$term == "insuranceyes"] < 1,
  nm_irr_zi$ratio[nm_irr_zi$term == "chronic"] > 1,
  nm_irr_zi$ratio[nm_irr_zi$term == "insuranceyes"] > 1,
  nm_irr_zi$ratio[nm_irr_zi$term == "school"] > 1)
# the bootstrap may not contradict the preference stated below: a
# conclusive non-rejection would need the discussion to be rewritten
if (boot_ok && boot$run_status == "COMPLETE" && boot$inference == "CONCLUSIVE") {
  stopifnot(isTRUE(boot$pool$reject))
}
```

**The data.** The NMES1988 data [@deb1997; @kleiber2008] come from the
1987–88 US National Medical Expenditure Survey and describe
`r f0(nm_desc$n)` people aged 66 and over. The response is `visits`, the
number of physician office visits. The covariates are `hospital` (the number
of hospital stays), `health` (self-perceived health: poor, average or
excellent, with average as the reference level), `chronic` (the number of
chronic conditions), `gender`, `school` (years of education) and `insurance`
(whether the person has private insurance). Both models use all six in the
count part. The ZINB zero part uses the handout's set, which is every
covariate except `health`; the check at the end of the model comparison
supports that choice.

**Descriptive evidence.** The mean number of visits is
`r f2(nm_desc$mean)` and the variance is `r f1(nm_desc$variance)`, about
`r f0(nm_desc$variance_to_mean)` times the mean. A Poisson distribution has
its variance equal to its mean, so the counts are strongly *overdispersed*:
they are far more spread out than a Poisson model allows.
`r f0(nm_desc$observed_zeros)` people (`r pct(nm_desc$observed_zero_share)`)
made no visits at all. As a first, rough look that ignores the covariates, a
single Poisson distribution with the sample mean would give
$e^{-`r f2(nm_desc$mean)`}$ = `r pct(nm_desc$poisson_unconditional_zero_share, 2)`
zeros, about `r f0(nm_desc$poisson_unconditional_zeros)` people
(@fig-visits, in the appendix). That comparison exaggerates the problem: people differ in
health, and a mixture of people with different means always has more zeros
and more spread than a single mean gives. The model comparison below
accounts for the covariates.

**Model comparison.** @tbl-nmes-compare compares the Poisson regression
(`glm()`) with our NB and ZINB fits; a model's expected zeros are the sum
over people of its fitted probability of zero visits.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nmes-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Model comparison for NMES1988. Expected zeros: the sum over people of each fitted model's probability of zero visits; observed zeros: 683. The last row adds `health` to the ZINB zero part (a sensitivity check)."
#| tbl-colwidths: false
kbl(data.frame(
  Model = nm_cmp$label,
  df = nm_cmp$df,
  `Log-likelihood` = f1(nm_cmp$loglik),
  AIC = f1(nm_cmp$AIC),
  BIC = f1(nm_cmp$BIC),
  `Expected zeros` = f1(nm_cmp$expected_zeros),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrrr")
```

Letting each person's mean depend on the covariates raises the Poisson
model's expected zeros from `r f0(nm_desc$poisson_unconditional_zeros)` (one
mean for everybody) to `r f0(cm("poisson", "expected_zeros"))`, which is
still a small fraction of the `r f0(nm_desc$observed_zeros)` observed. The
Poisson model is also far worse than the NB model in log-likelihood: the
likelihood-ratio test for overdispersion gives LR =
`r f0(nm_od$statistic)` (p `r format.pval(nm_od$p.value, eps = 1e-16)`;
the p-value accounts for theta = infinity being the boundary of the NB
model). The NB model, with $\hat\theta$ = `r f2(nm_th_nb[["theta"]])`
(95% profile interval `r ci2(nm_th_nb[["profile_lower"]], nm_th_nb[["profile_upper"]])`),
predicts `r f0(cm("nb", "expected_zeros"))` zeros: overdispersion alone
accounts for most of the zeros, but about
`r f0(nm_desc$observed_zeros - cm("nb", "expected_zeros"))` are still
missing. The ZINB model predicts `r f0(cm("zinb", "expected_zeros"))`, about
`r f0(cm("zinb", "expected_zeros") - nm_desc$observed_zeros)` too many,
a smaller error in the other direction. ZINB also has the lower AIC (by
`r f1(cm("nb", "AIC") - cm("zinb", "AIC"))`) and, despite BIC's larger
penalty for its `r cm("zinb", "df") - cm("nb", "df")` extra parameters, the
lower BIC (by `r f1(cm("nb", "BIC") - cm("zinb", "BIC"))`). Adding `health`
to the zero part raises the log-likelihood by only
`r f2(cm("zinb_health", "loglik") - cm("zinb", "loglik"))` for two more
parameters, and makes both AIC and BIC worse, so the smaller zero model is
kept.

@fig-rootogram shows the fit at every count: each observed frequency hangs
from the model's expected frequency (square-root scale), so a bar ending
below the dashed line marks a count the model under-predicts, and one ending
above it a count it over-predicts. The Poisson model misses everywhere.
The NB model has a specific pattern at the low end: too few zeros and too
many people with one or two visits (`r f0(-gap("nb", 1))` and
`r f0(-gap("nb", 2))` too many). The ZINB model removes most of that
pattern, and its total absolute error over the counts 1 to 30 is
`r f0(abs_err("zinb"))`, against `r f0(abs_err("nb"))` for NB.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rootogram
#| fig-cap: "Hanging rootograms: observed frequencies (bars) hanging from each model's expected frequencies (red points), on a square-root scale, for 0 to 30 visits. The NB and ZINB panels share one vertical scale; the Poisson panel needs a wider one."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.4
y_range <- function(t) {
  s <- seq_len(nrow(t) - 1L)
  range(0, sqrt(t$expected[s]) - sqrt(t$observed[s]), sqrt(t$expected[s]))
}
yl_nb <- range(y_range(nm_tabs$nb), y_range(nm_tabs$zinb))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5), cex = 0.7)
nmes_rootogram_panel(nm_tabs$poisson, "Poisson regression")
nmes_rootogram_panel(nm_tabs$nb, "NB", ylim = yl_nb)
nmes_rootogram_panel(nm_tabs$zinb, "ZINB", ylim = yl_nb)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: nmes-boot-text
#| include: false
# The bootstrap paragraph reports what the saved run found. It separates
# two questions: did the run finish (run status), and can the test decide
# (inference)? An inconclusive test is reported with its reasons and is
# not used as evidence either way.
boot_text <- if (!boot_ok) {
  "The bootstrap results have not been produced yet."
} else if (boot$run_status != "COMPLETE") {
  sprintf("The bootstrap run did not complete (%s), so no result is reported.",
          paste(boot$run_reasons, collapse = "; "))
} else {
  pl <- boot$pool
  base <- sprintf(paste(
    "In the parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio test, %s data sets were",
    "simulated from the fitted NB model, and both models were refitted to",
    "each. %s of them could not be refitted reliably (failed replicates).",
    "Of the %s usable replicates, %s had a likelihood-ratio statistic at",
    "least as large as the observed LR = %s, which gives p = %s. Counting",
    "every failed replicate as below the observed value, or as at or above",
    "it, puts p between %s and %s."),
    f0(boot$settings$B), f0(pl$failures), f0(pl$used), if (pl$exceed == 0) "none" else pl$exceed,
    f1(boot$observed$statistic), format(signif(pl$p.value, 2)),
    format(signif(pl$p.bounds[["lower"]], 2)),
    format(signif(pl$p.bounds[["upper"]], 2)))
  verdict <- if (boot$inference == "CONCLUSIVE") {
    if (isTRUE(pl$reject)) {
      "The test is conclusive and rejects the NB model in favour of ZINB at the 5% level."
    } else {
      "The test is conclusive and does not reject the NB model at the 5% level."
    }
  } else {
    sprintf(paste(
      "The test is **inconclusive**: %s. It therefore cannot decide",
      "between NB and ZINB, and no conclusion is drawn from it."),
      paste(boot$inference_reasons, collapse = "; "))
  }
  paste(base, verdict)
}
boot_note <- if (boot_ok && !is.null(boot$maxit_decision)) {
  sprintf(paste(
    "The refits used the EM iteration limit maxit = %d, chosen before the",
    "full run by a fixed rule that looks only at the share of failed",
    "replicates in 50-replicate pilots: %s at the default maxit = 5000 and",
    "%s at maxit = 20000; the lower share wins, the default on a tie."),
    boot$settings$maxit, pct(boot$maxit_decision$share_default),
    if (is.na(boot$maxit_decision$share_high)) "not run" else
      pct(boot$maxit_decision$share_high))
} else ""
```

A formal test of NB against ZINB is harder than it looks, because the NB
model is the edge of the ZINB model (a zero-inflation probability of 0, with
the zero-part intercept at minus infinity), and the usual chi-squared
reference for a likelihood-ratio test does not hold on such a boundary. The
Vuong statistics [@vuong1989], z = `r f1(nm_vu$statistic[["Raw"]])` (raw),
`r f1(nm_vu$statistic[["AIC-corrected"]])` (AIC-corrected) and
`r f1(nm_vu$statistic[["BIC-corrected"]])` (BIC-corrected), all favour ZINB,
but for the same reason they are descriptive here, not a test.
`r boot_text``r if (nzchar(boot_note)) paste0("^[", boot_note, "]") else ""`

**Interpretation.** @tbl-nmes-irr gives the count-part effects as
*incidence rate ratios* (IRRs): the factor by which the expected number of
visits is multiplied per unit of a covariate (or against the reference level
of a factor), holding the others fixed; in ZINB it describes the people "at
risk" of visiting a physician.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nmes-irr
#| tbl-cap: "Count part: incidence rate ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals, for the NB model and the ZINB count part."
#| tbl-colwidths: false
irr_cell <- function(e) sprintf("%s (%s, %s)", f2(e$ratio), f2(e$lower), f2(e$upper))
kbl(data.frame(
  Covariate = nm_irr_nb$term,
  `NB IRR (95% CI)` = irr_cell(nm_irr_nb),
  `ZINB count IRR (95% CI)` = irr_cell(nm_irr_zi[match(nm_irr_nb$term, nm_irr_zi$term), ]),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lcc")
```

```{r}
#| label: nmes-effects-text
#| include: false
irr <- function(term) nm_irr_zi[nm_irr_zi$term == term, ]
or <- function(term) nm_or[nm_or$term == term, ]
change <- function(r) sprintf("%s%% %s", f0(100 * abs(r - 1)),
                              if (r > 1) "more" else "fewer")
odds_change <- function(r) sprintf("%s%% %s", f0(100 * abs(r - 1)),
                                   if (r > 1) "higher" else "lower")
eff <- function(e) sprintf("%s (95%% CI %s)", f2(e$ratio), ci2(e$lower, e$upper))
```

In the ZINB model every count-part effect is clearly different from 1. Each
additional hospital stay multiplies the expected number of visits by
`r eff(irr("hospital"))`, about `r change(irr("hospital")$ratio)` visits,
and each additional chronic condition by `r eff(irr("chronic"))`. Compared
with average health, poor health goes with
`r change(irr("healthpoor")$ratio)` visits and excellent health with
`r change(irr("healthexcellent")$ratio)`. Men make
`r change(irr("gendermale")$ratio)` visits than women, each year of
education adds `r f0(100 * (irr("school")$ratio - 1))`%, and private
insurance `r f0(100 * (irr("insuranceyes")$ratio - 1))`% (intervals in
@tbl-nmes-irr). The NB estimates point the same way and are all further
from 1: without a separate group of non-users, the NB model has to fit those
people's zeros through the same covariate effects.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nmes-or
#| tbl-cap: "ZINB zero part: odds ratios of being a structural zero (a person who would make no visits in any case), with 95% Wald confidence intervals."
#| tbl-colwidths: false
kbl(data.frame(
  Covariate = nm_or$term,
  `OR (95% CI)` = irr_cell(nm_or),
  `p-value` = format.pval(nm_or$p_value, digits = 2, eps = 1e-4),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lcc")
```

The zero part needs care in reading. It models the probability $\pi_i$
that a person is a **structural zero**: someone who would make no physician
office visits in any case, a "non-user". The odds ratios in @tbl-nmes-or are
therefore ratios of the odds of *belonging to the non-user group*. They are
not odds ratios of observing zero visits. A person can also make no visits
in the period while being at risk, by chance, so the probability of an
observed zero combines both parts,
$P(Y_i = 0) = \pi_i + (1 - \pi_i)\, f_{\mathrm{NB}}(0; \mu_i, \theta)$,
and a covariate's effect on it depends on both its odds ratio and its IRR.
With that in mind: each additional chronic condition multiplies the odds of
being a non-user by `r eff(or("chronic"))`, and private insurance by
`r eff(or("insuranceyes"))`; men have `r f2(or("gendermale")$ratio)` times
the odds of women, and each year of education multiplies them by
`r f2(or("school")$ratio)`. The hospital-stay odds ratio is not significant
at the 5% level (p = `r f2(or("hospital")$p_value)`). Chronic illness and
insurance thus work in the same direction in both parts: less likely to be
a non-user and, among users, more visits. Among users the counts stay
overdispersed: $\hat\theta$ = `r f2(nm_th_zi[["theta"]])` (95% Wald
interval `r ci2(nm_th_zi[["wald_lower"]], nm_th_zi[["wald_upper"]])`,
profile interval `r ci2(nm_th_zi[["profile_lower"]], nm_th_zi[["profile_upper"]])`).

**Which model?** The Poisson model is clearly inadequate: it cannot produce
counts this spread out, and the overdispersion test rejects it decisively.
The choice between NB and ZINB rests on several pieces of evidence that
point the same way without any one being decisive alone. Both information
criteria favour ZINB, and BIC does so although it penalizes the six extra
parameters heavily. The NB model's errors have a systematic shape (too few
zeros, too many ones and twos), which is what a separate group of non-users
would produce, and the ZINB model removes most of it. The zero-part effects
are large, mostly precisely estimated and plausible: people with chronic
conditions or private insurance are much less likely never to see a
physician. Against that, ZINB slightly over-predicts the zeros, so it is not
a perfect description either, and its split of the zeros into structural and
chance zeros depends on its assumptions (a logistic model for the non-users
and an NB distribution for the users); the data cannot verify that split
directly. `r if (boot_ok && boot$run_status == "COMPLETE") (if (boot$inference == "CONCLUSIVE") "The bootstrap test agrees with this assessment." else "The bootstrap test could not settle the question, so the preference rests on the information criteria and the fit at each count.") else ""`
On balance we prefer the **ZINB model**, mainly for its better fit at the
low counts and its interpretable two-part structure. All the effects are
associations in a 1987–88 survey of people aged 66 and over, not causal
effects, and they need not carry over to other populations.


## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: discussion-guards
#| include: false
# Claim guards for the qualitative statements below.
stopifnot(is.na(ratio_bc) || ratio_bc > 1, is.na(ratio_nm) || ratio_nm > 1,
          # "standard errors that match the actual spread"
          !sim_ok || (ratio_range[1] >= 0.9 && ratio_range[2] <= 1.1),
          all(req$passed))
```

Both models are fitted by IRLS, Newton–Raphson and EM without a
general-purpose optimizer, reproduce `glm.nb()` and `zeroinfl()` well within
the required tolerances (@sec-benchmark), and `zinbreg()` recovers known
parameters with accurate standard errors (@sec-simulation).

**Limitations.**

* *Speed.* EM converges linearly, so `zinbreg()` is several times slower
  than `zeroinfl()` (@sec-benchmark); this matters when the model is
  refitted many times, as in the bootstrap test (@sec-nmes).
* *Wald intervals* rely on approximately normal estimates, which holds less
  well for the zero-part coefficients and $\theta$ at moderate sample
  sizes; `confint()` offers a profile interval for $\theta$.
* *The simulation* used one design and one sample size with the correct
  model; it does not show behaviour under misspecification or weak zero
  inflation.
* *Testing NB against ZINB* is a boundary problem, so the standard
  likelihood-ratio and Vuong tests do not apply; the parametric bootstrap
  test is valid but slow, and some refits fail, which the package reports
  as bounds rather than dropping them.
* *Local maxima.* Excess zeros can be explained by zero inflation or by
  overdispersion, so the ZINB likelihood can have several maxima. The
  gradient check establishes only approximate stationarity (with the
  curvature condition, a local maximum), not the global maximum.
  `r if (length(local_max)) sprintf("In the simulation, %s stopped at a local maximum, which confint() detected.", if (length(local_max) == 1L) "one fit" else paste(length(local_max), "fits")) else ""`
  Several starting values would guard against this.

**Possible extensions.** Hurdle models; EM acceleration (for example
Newton steps near the maximum with the analytic Hessian the package already
computes); sandwich standard errors; and simulations that vary the sample
size, the strength of zero inflation and the model specification.

## Outline — to be written by the author before submission

This section must be written by the author in their own words. The points
the project requires, and candidate examples from `dev/ai_use_log.md`, are
listed below as a starting point; delete this box when the statement is
written.
:::

**Required points.**

1. What Claude Code was asked to do (planning, implementation, tests,
   benchmark and simulation scripts, the report).
2. What was verified independently (equations checked against the project
   description; comparisons with `glm.nb()` and `zeroinfl()`; tests; the
   prohibited-function check; reading the code).
3. At least one concrete example where Claude's output had to be corrected
   or rejected.

**Candidate examples from the log** (choose and describe in your own words):

* *2026-11-08, `nbreg()` plan:* Claude's first plan clipped $\eta$ and
  floored $\mu$, which would have silently changed the likelihood; it also
  used the number of positive-weight observations instead of the sum of the
  weights in the starting value for $\theta$.
* *2026-11-09, `zinbreg()` validation:* with weights, `zeroinfl()` disagreed
  with `zinbreg()` by 0.03; instead of relaxing the tolerance, the
  investigation showed that `zeroinfl()`'s weighted fit stops at a point that
  is not a maximum.
* *2026-11-09, `grad_tol`:* the planned tolerance of $10^{-6}$ could have
  allowed errors above the required $10^{-3}$ on bioChemists, and was changed
  to $10^{-8}$ on that evidence.

#| label: tbl-bench-time

if (is.null(saved)) {
  cat("The saved timings were not found in the installed package; run inst/benchmark/benchmark.R.")
} else {
  tm <- saved$timing
  tm <- tm[!grepl("numeric Hessian", tm$fit), ]
  tm$fit <- sub(", analytic Hessian", "", tm$fit)
  kbl(data.frame(
    Data = tm$data_name, Model = tm$model, Fit = tm$fit,
    `Median (s)` = formatC(tm$median_s, digits = 3, format = "g"),
    `Range (s)` = sprintf("%s to %s", formatC(tm$min_s, digits = 3, format = "g"),
                          formatC(tm$max_s, digits = 3, format = "g")),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "lllrr")
}

### Provenance of the saved results {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\sloppy
```

The timings, the simulation and the NMES1988 bootstrap are read from
saved results, because they take minutes to hours to produce. Each was
produced from a clean, committed state of the package, and each is
checked here against the installed code.

**Timings.** `r if (!is.null(p)) sprintf("The timings were measured on %s (%s, %s cores) under %s, with MASS %s, pscl %s and bench %s, on %s, for the package code of commit %s (code fingerprint %s; provenance %s).", p$os, p$cpu, p$cores, p$r_version, p$versions[['MASS']], p$versions[['pscl']], p$versions[['bench']], substr(p$date, 1, 10), substr(p$git_commit, 1, 7), p$fingerprint_installed, p$status) else ""`
`r if (!is.null(prov_check)) (if (prov_check$status == "matches") prov_check$message else paste0("**", prov_check$message, "**")) else ""`

**Simulation.** `r if (sim_ok) sprintf("The results were produced at commit %s (code fingerprint %s; provenance %s) under %s.", substr(sim_prov$git_commit, 1, 7), sim_prov$fingerprint_installed, sim_prov$status, sim_prov$r_version)`
`r if (sim_ok) (if (sim_check$status == "matches") sim_check$message else paste0("**", sim_check$message, "**")) else ""`

**NMES1988 bootstrap.** `r if (boot_ok) sprintf("The bootstrap results were produced at commit %s (code fingerprint %s; provenance %s) under %s.", substr(boot$provenance$git_commit, 1, 7), boot$provenance$fingerprint_installed, boot$provenance$status, boot$provenance$r_version)`
`r if (boot_ok) (if (boot_check$status == "matches") boot_check$message else paste0("**", boot_check$message, "**")) else ""`

```{r}
#| label: fig-visits
#| fig-cap: "Observed frequencies of physician office visits (bars) and the frequencies a single Poisson distribution with the sample mean would give (points). The single Poisson ignores the covariates; it is a descriptive reference only."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.6
fr <- nm_desc$freq
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 0.5, 0.5))
bp <- barplot(fr$observed, names.arg = fr$visits, col = "grey80",
              border = "grey40", las = 2, cex.names = 0.7,
              ylim = c(0, 1.05 * max(fr$observed, fr$poisson_unconditional)),
              xlab = "Physician office visits (30+ = 30 or more)",
              ylab = "Number of people")
points(bp, fr$poisson_unconditional, pch = 19, col = "firebrick", cex = 0.7)
legend("topright", c("Observed", "Single Poisson with the sample mean"),
       pch = c(22, 19), pt.bg = c("grey80", NA), pt.cex = c(1.6, 0.8),
       col = c("grey40", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-z
#| fig-cap: "Standardized errors (estimate − truth) / SE for each parameter over the usable replications. If the estimates are approximately normal and the standard errors are right, about 95% of them lie between the dashed lines at ±1.96."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
if (sim_ok) {
  rep <- sim$replicates[sim$replicates$class == "usable", ]
  pn <- ss$parameter
  zs <- lapply(pn, function(p) {
    (rep[[paste0("estimate_", p)]] - sim$truth$params[[p]]) /
      rep[[paste0("se_", p)]]
  })
  op <- graphics::par(mar = c(6.5, 4, 1, 1))
  graphics::boxplot(zs, names = pn, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.8, outcex = 0.4,
                    ylab = "(estimate - truth) / SE", col = "grey85")
  graphics::abline(h = c(-1.96, 0, 1.96), lty = c(2, 1, 2),
                   col = c("firebrick", "grey40", "firebrick"))
  graphics::par(op)
}
```
